column4: The section’s field chain begins with wind and rain reaching dead land. This ayah says the winds carry heavy clouds to a dead land, where water brings forth fruits; it supplies the rain-to-yield movement immediately before the soil contrast in 7:58.

The section’s image asks what sustained care can make grow, while its kenūd gloss names a cut bond. This ayah compares a good word to a tree with firm roots and high branches, joining rootedness and fruitful speech.

The section says the yield of good soil is what care brings to completion. This ayah says the tree bears fruit by its Lord’s permission in every season, making ongoing yield a picture of granted care.

The section describes both a severed gratitude bond and land that bears nothing. This ayah compares a bad word to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, a direct reversal of rooted, fruitful continuity.

The section depicts land receiving rain and producing provision, then the human forgetting its giver. This ayah says God made the earth a resting place, sent down water, and brought forth fruits as provision, before warning against setting up rivals to Him.

The section’s kenūd soil yields nothing despite rain. This ayah compares showy or injurious giving to a smooth rock with a thin covering of soil that rain leaves bare, making failed generosity resemble a field unable to retain its yield.

The section names grain as the expected yield and خير as gift or generosity. This ayah tells people to spend from the good things they earn and from what God brings forth from the earth, joining harvest to a generous return.

The section’s field image presents a cultivated yield as a gift that can be lost. This ayah pictures a garden destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and dependent, making the security of provision fragile.

The section’s soil image concerns what land yields under care. This ayah introduces a man given two gardens of grapes, surrounded by palms and crops, a specific instance of received agricultural abundance.
The section’s word حبّ names love and خير can mean wealth or gift. This ayah’s garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, turning received abundance into self-regard.

The section says a person forgets the giver while clinging to what he has received. This ayah shows the garden owner wronging himself and assuming his garden will never perish, treating provision as secure in itself.

The section’s surah context asks whether the human knows he will be raised and his inward contents exposed. This ayah’s garden owner doubts the Hour and presumes he will receive something better if returned to his Lord, exposing confidence in wealth against accountability.

The section’s Rab gloss describes one who nurtures and forms through stages. The garden owner’s companion answers that the Lord created him from dust, then a drop, then formed him as a man; it grounds human life in received creation.

The section says a recipient forgets the source of his garden-like provision. The companion tells the owner to say “ما شاء الله لا قوة إلا بالله” on entering his garden, giving words for recognizing the giver and one’s dependence.

The section’s good-soil image can be reversed into a land that fails. This ayah has the companion warn that God may give him a better garden and send a calamity upon the other, making the yield’s dependence on God explicit.

The section’s dictionary gloss for ن ق ع includes gathered water and its field depends on rain. This ayah warns that the garden’s water may sink into the earth so its owner cannot recover it, showing how the water that sustains yield is not his possession.

The section says the human is ungrateful to his Rabb despite provision. This ayah’s garden owner sees his crop ruined, regrets what he spent, and wishes he had not associated anyone with his Lord; loss makes the forgotten relation visible.

The section says the Rabb remains the one who knows and sustains those who cut the bond. After the garden is destroyed, this ayah says the owner has no group to help him against God, showing the limit of human control over received provision.

The section names Rabb as owner and master. This ayah concludes the garden account by placing true protection with God and the better reward and outcome with Him, restoring the ownership the garden owner ignored.

The section describes rain, soil, and expected growth. This ayah pictures rain-fed vegetation mixing, then drying and scattering as debris, a repeated field image that adds the passing of a crop to the section’s account of provision.

The section describes a person severing gratitude after gifts arrive. This ayah recounts people who promise that if God gives them from His bounty they will give charity and be righteous, making the promised return explicit.
The section says the recipient cuts the return of gratitude. This ayah says that once they receive from God’s bounty, they become stingy and turn away, matching the break between gift and thanks.
The section says the Rabb knows those who fail to honor the bond. This ayah describes the lasting hypocrisy in their hearts after they broke their promise, showing a breach that remains known to God.

The section depicts the human as ungrateful to the Rabb and intensely attached to خير. This ayah says that if people possessed the treasures of their Lord’s mercy, they would withhold them for fear of spending, directly naming the stinginess that blocks reciprocity.
The section says the human forgets the Rabb behind his gifts. This ayah says the Lord has bounty toward people but most do not give thanks, a direct formulation of the section’s central relation.

The section says a person forgets the Rabb who provides and nurtures. This ayah asks people to remember God’s favor and asks who provides from heaven and earth, directing attention from provision back to its giver.
The section’s field imagery treats water as a gift needed for growth. This ayah asks people to consider the water they drink, opening the passage that questions its source.
The section names clouds and rain as part of the field’s care. This ayah asks whether people bring drinking water down from the rain clouds or God does, placing the source beyond the recipient.

The section describes people receiving good and cutting off thanks. This ayah asks whether they make their provision an act of denial, explicitly turning provision into the point at which gratitude is withheld.

The section calls kenūd ingratitude for the provision one receives. This ayah says people favored with provision do not pass it on to those under their authority and asks whether they deny God’s favor, making withheld sharing a form of denial.

The section’s Rab gloss includes owner and provider. This ayah names spouses, children, and good provision given by God, then asks whether people believe in falsehood and deny His favor; it extends the gift relation from food to family.

The section’s K-N-D dictionary gloss includes refusal to maintain closeness. This ayah praises those who join what God commanded to be joined, a direct contrary pattern to the bond the section says kenūd cuts.
The section says خير includes generosity and a gift’s proper response. This ayah describes feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, turning attachment into generous giving.

The section asks what connects a recipient to the giver after provision. This ayah says the givers act only for God’s sake and seek neither repayment nor thanks, clarifying the motive that kenūd lacks.

The section links love of خير with gratitude and maintaining a bond. This ayah describes righteousness as giving beloved wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy, while keeping promises; it joins generosity to sustained obligations.

The section depicts ingratitude toward the Rabb as a broken response. This ayah asks what God would gain by punishing people if they are grateful and believe, stating the significance of the response without the section’s field imagery.

The section’s field chain joins rain, revived land, and the human response to the giver. This ayah asks who sends water and revives earth after death; the answer is God, while most people fail to understand, joining recognition to the scene.

The section builds a field image from rain and land. This ayah names rain from the sky that revives the earth after its death among God’s signs, showing how the yield can call the recipient to recognize its source.

The section says gifts are completed by the Rabb and can be met with gratitude. This ayah says whatever people spend, God replaces it and is the best provider, making provision and return a continuing relation.

The section’s خير gloss includes generosity, while its kenūd figure withholds the return. This ayah says a rightful share in wealth belongs to the petitioner and deprived person, making generosity a concrete response to provision.
The section’s human loves خير but may fail to return it. This ayah describes a known share in the wealth of the people who pray, giving a specific form to generosity.

The section’s K-N-D gloss includes neglecting what should be returned. This ayah identifies the recipients of that share as the petitioner and deprived person, specifying who the generous response reaches.

The section describes Rabb as the one who repairs and land as the recipient of nurturing. This ayah forbids corruption after the earth has been set right and says God’s mercy is near to those who do good, reversing the kenūd refusal of care.

The section’s Rab gloss includes the one who improves, while kenūd land bears no growth. This ayah depicts a person who spreads corruption and destroys crops and offspring, a human reversal of the Rabb’s nurturing work.
The section’s low-land gloss describes rainwater gathering in earth. This ayah asks who could bring flowing water if it sank away, making dependence on retained water explicit.

The section asks the recipient to acknowledge the Rabb behind provision. This ayah contributes the call to seek forgiveness; 71:11 supplies the promised rain, so the adjacent verses connect a return to God with renewed provision.
The section places Rabb before the charge of ingratitude. This ayah asks why people do not attribute due greatness to God, directly addressing the failure to honor the one named as Rabb.

The section says people in the graves will be raised and their Lord knows them. This ayah says God knows what the earth consumes of them and has a preserving record, joining the grave to divine knowledge.

The section’s witness may be the human or the Rabb, and its final ayah places the reckoning on that day. This ayah says every soul comes with a driver and a witness, making the accountability scene explicit.
The section says what is hidden in chests will be brought to light. This ayah describes the veil being removed and a person’s sight becoming sharp, a concrete image of disclosure on the day.

The section says the human forgets favors while the Rabb remains fully informed. This ayah says God will inform people of what they did, which He counted while they forgot, making the contrast between human forgetting and divine knowledge exact.

The section says the human will be raised and the Rabb will be fully informed on that day. This ayah depicts every community kneeling and summoned to its record, placing the account in a public judgment scene.
The section says the Rabb knows those who cut the gratitude bond. This ayah presents a truthful record of everything people did, making the knowledge of their acts concrete.
The section says that on the day of reckoning the Rabb remains fully informed. This ayah shows the earth illuminated, the record set down, and witnesses brought, a direct scene of judgment.
The section’s 100:11 says the Rabb is fully informed of people on that day. This ayah says every soul is repaid for what it did and God knows best what they do, joining knowledge to just recompense.

The section’s surah context asks whether the human knows what will be exposed after the graves are opened. This ayah says each person’s record is attached to him and brought out on resurrection day, making accountability individual.
The section says the human is witness to his own response. This ayah tells the person to read his record and says he is sufficient as his own reckoner, directly joining self-witness to the record.

The section’s surah context says what is in the chests will be brought to light. This ayah says the human will be informed of what he sent ahead and left behind, specifying what the reckoning reveals.

The section says no one escapes the Rabb’s knowledge on that day. This ayah says people will be exposed and none of their secrets will remain hidden, directly matching the disclosure of inward contents.
The section says the buried will be raised and what is concealed will be exposed. This ayah says the records will be spread open, a direct judgment-day disclosure.
The section says the Rabb is fully informed and the contents of chests will be exposed. This ayah says every soul will know what it has brought forward, connecting disclosure to personal deeds.
The section says the human will be raised and brought to account. This ayah describes the person who receives his record in his right hand, a specific form of that accounting.

The section’s final ayah places the Rabb’s knowledge on the day of reckoning. This ayah promises an easy account; 84:9 supplies the return to family, while this row contributes the ease of the reckoning.
The section asks whether the human knows that he will be raised and exposed. This ayah describes the record-holder returning joyful to his family, a concrete result of the reckoning.

The section says the human’s inward contents will be disclosed and the Rabb knows all. This ayah describes a person receiving his record behind his back, the contrary outcome to the right-hand record in 84:7.
The section says the human will face the result of what he concealed and did. This ayah gives the record-holder’s response of calling for destruction, a particular reaction to disclosure.
The section’s image ends with the Rabb fully informed on that day. This ayah names the record-holder’s destination in the blazing fire, a specific consequence of the account.
The section describes human attachment to worldly good and later exposure. This ayah says the person had been joyful among his family, contrasting ease before death with the judgment that follows.
The section asks whether a person knows he will be raised. This ayah says the person thought he would never return to God, naming the ignorance that the section challenges.
The section says the Rabb is fully informed about people on that day. This ayah says the Lord was ever seeing him, directly grounding the reckoning in divine awareness.

The section says the Rabb is fully informed on the day and allows the earth to serve as a witness. This ayah says the earth’s report comes by its Lord’s inspiration; 99:4 supplies the report itself, while this row explains its source.
The section says the contents of the graves and chests will be brought out. This ayah says people will emerge in separate groups to be shown their deeds, completing the disclosure scene.

The section pairs intense love of خير with the opening of graves. This ayah says rivalry in accumulating more distracts people, connecting the section’s attachment to wealth with its warning about what lies beyond the grave.

The section’s 100:8-9 moves from love of good to the graves being opened. This ayah says rivalry lasts until people visit the graves, supplying a close parallel between wealth-seeking and delayed awareness.
The section says the Rabb will be fully informed about people on that day. This ayah says people will be questioned about نعيم, directly connecting received favor to the reckoning.
